title: Orebić Cost Guide 2027: Prices for Stay, Food, Ferry
metaDescription: Orebić prices for 2027 planning: apartments from about €30, ferry to Korčula €2.50–4.40, kitesurf courses, food and daily budgets in euros.
content:
## How Much Does a Trip to Orebić Cost?

Orebić, on the southern coast of the Pelješac peninsula, costs noticeably less than Dubrovnik (about 100 km by road) or Korčula Old Town, which sits across the channel. Most visitors stay in private apartments, eat out once a day and take the ferry across to Korčula at least once. A realistic daily budget per person, with two sharing a room:

| Style | Daily cost per person (peak season) | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| Budget | €60–80 | Studio apartment, self-catering breakfast and lunch, one simple dinner, ferry trips |
| Mid-range | €100–150 | Nicer apartment near the promenade, restaurant dinners with wine, a day trip or two |
| Comfortable | €200+ | Beachfront resort or villa, boat trips, water-sports lessons |

These are planning estimates built from current accommodation rates and typical Dalmatian restaurant pricing. Shoulder months (May, June, September) cut accommodation by roughly 20–30%.

## Accommodation Prices in Orebić

### Private apartments and studios

Apartments dominate the Orebić market. Small family-run properties list studios for two from about €30–42 per night in the low and shoulder season; one local operator shows a 2-person studio from €32 and a 3+2 apartment from €72 on a September date, with tourist tax and cleaning included in that rate. Another operator near the water lists studios from €49 in low season, €59 in shoulder season and €69 in high season.

Across major booking platforms, the average apartment in Orebić comes out around the equivalent of €110–120 per night, but that figure is skewed upward by large villas and beachfront units. Vacation-home listings that include villas with pools average roughly €150 per night, and larger villas for up to 10 guests start above €500 per night.

### Hotels and resorts

Orebić has few traditional hotels. Mid-range 3-star stays average roughly €140 per night on booking platforms and 4-star about €230. The beachfront Bellevue Maradiso Village by Aminess sits at the top of the market, with peak-season rates well above €400 per night.

### Tourist tax

A small per-person nightly tourist tax is added by most hosts unless the quoted price already includes it. Check whether a listed rate is "all-in" before comparing.

### Insider tip on booking

Timing matters more than property type. A studio that costs €35 in late May can cost €70 or more in the last two weeks of July. Orebić's water is still warm in late September, and Jadrolinija and G&V Line Iadera both switch to cheaper off-season fares on 28 September.

## Ferry and Transport Costs

### Passenger ferry to Korčula Town

The passenger boat run by G&V Line Iadera (line 614) crosses in about 15 minutes and lands right in Korčula Old Town. Fares in 2026 were €2.50 off-season (1 January–28 May and 28 September–31 December) and €3.40–3.50 in season (29 May–27 September). Children aged 3–12 pay €1.50. Departures run roughly hourly from about 05:20, and in high season the last boats go late in the evening. Pay on board or at the quay; carry cash.

### Car ferry to Dominče

The Jadrolinija car ferry (line 634) takes about 20 minutes and docks at Dominče, roughly 3 km from Korčula Old Town. Adults pay €2.50 off-season and €4.40 in peak season. A standard car up to 5.0 m long and 2.0 m high pays €10.40 off-season and €16.20 in peak season. Prices are the same in both directions.

Taking the car over rarely makes sense for a day trip. Korčula Old Town has tight parking, and the passenger boat drops you at the gate. Leave the car in Orebić and walk on.

### Driving to Orebić and tolls

Since the Pelješac Bridge opened in 2022, the drive from Zagreb no longer needs the Ploče–Trpanj ferry. The toll from Zagreb to the Karamatići exit for Orebić is about €33.70. The old Ploče–Trpanj ferry still runs, at €25.20 per car and €6.70 per adult, but the bridge saves both money and time.

### Local taxis

A taxi from Orebić to Viganj (7 km) costs about €15. Orebić is compact enough that most visitors walk everywhere along the waterfront.

## Food and Drink Prices

Orebić restaurant prices follow typical southern Dalmatian levels, and are lower than Dubrovnik or Korčula Old Town. Typical ranges in summer:

- Coffee or espresso: €1.50–2.50
- Local beer (0.5 L) at a café: €3.50–5
- Glass of Pelješac wine: €3.50–6
- Pizza or pasta: €10–15
- Grilled fish or seafood main: €18–30; fish by weight is the main cost driver
- Cuttlefish risotto or tuna steak: roughly €15–28
- Groceries: a full day of self-catering for one person often stays under €15

Price differences between a beach bar and a sit-down restaurant are small in Orebić. A recent traveler account noted that the same dish cost about the same at a beach shack and at a restaurant in town, so choose by view and atmosphere instead of expecting a discount at casual places.

### Insider tip on wine

Pelješac is Croatia's main Plavac Mali region. Buying a bottle directly from a winery or a local shop usually costs well below restaurant markups. Order the house Plavac by the glass at dinner and buy bottles to take home elsewhere.

## Activities and Extras

### Kitesurfing and windsurfing in Viganj

Viganj, 7 km west of Orebić, is the main wind-sports village on the peninsula. The afternoon maestral usually arrives around 14:00 from June to August. Current school pricing includes:

- Beginner 12-hour kitesurfing course at Water Donkey: €340 (4–5 days, radio helmets, speedboat, equipment included)
- Private kitesurfing lesson, 1 hour: €69
- Another Orebić-area school lists a 12-hour (6-lesson) course at €495, a 6-hour course at €260 and a 2-hour lesson at €95

Prices vary by school and season, so compare what is included (equipment, boat support, insurance) before booking. Lessons are usually arranged a few hours ahead by phone because wind strength decides the schedule.

### Beaches and hiking

Orebić's town beaches are free. Sun loungers and umbrellas, where offered, usually cost roughly €10–20 per set for the day in summer. Hiking up Mount Sveti Ilija costs nothing.

## Sample Budgets

### 3 days, budget, two people, June

- Accommodation: 3 nights × €45 = €135
- Ferry to Korčula (2 adults return): about €14
- Food: about €60/day for two = €180
- Total: roughly €330 for two (about €165 per person)

### 7 days, mid-range, two people, July

- Accommodation: 7 nights × €90 = €630
- Ferry trips (three return trips for two): about €42
- Food and drinks: about €110/day for two = €770
- Activities and extras: about €150
- Total: roughly €1,600 for two

## Money-Saving Tips

1. Travel in the second half of September. The off-season ferry fare starts 28 September, and apartment rates drop before that.
2. Book apartments directly with the owner when possible. Several family properties publish all-in rates with tourist tax and cleaning included.
3. Skip the car ferry. The passenger boat costs under €4 and lands in the Old Town.
4. Self-cater breakfast and lunch; keep restaurant meals for dinner.
5. Carry cash for the ferry and small cafés, even though the euro is Croatia's currency and most restaurants take cards.

The common advice to "stay on Korčula and day-trip to Orebić" looks cheaper on paper, but it rarely is: Korčula Old Town apartments cost more, parking is difficult, and Orebić has the better beach and quieter evenings. Staying in Orebić and commuting by the €2.50–3.50 passenger boat is the better value.

faq.question: How much does a day in Orebić cost?
faq.answer: A budget traveler can spend about €60–80 per person per day in summer, including an apartment share, simple meals and a ferry ride. Mid-range travelers should plan €100–150 per person. Prices fall in May and late September.

faq.question: How much is the ferry from Orebić to Korčula?
faq.answer: The passenger boat to Korčula Old Town costs €2.50 off-season and about €3.40–3.50 in season (29 May–27 September), and the crossing takes about 15 minutes. The car ferry to Dominče costs €2.50–4.40 per adult, plus €10.40–16.20 for a standard car.

faq.question: Is Orebić cheaper than Korčula Town?
faq.answer: Generally yes. Orebić has more small apartments with studios starting around €30–50 per night in the low and shoulder season, while Korčula Old Town has fewer rooms and higher rates. Restaurant prices are similar to slightly lower in Orebić.

faq.question: How much does an apartment in Orebić cost per night?
faq.answer: Simple studios for two start from about €30–42 in shoulder season and about €69 in peak season at small family properties. Larger apartments commonly cost €70–130, and villas with pools go from about €400 to over €500 per night.

faq.question: How much does a kitesurfing course in Viganj cost?
faq.answer: A 12-hour beginner kitesurfing course at Water Donkey costs €340, and a private one-hour lesson costs €69. Other schools in the Orebić area list 12-hour courses at about €495. Check that equipment and boat support are included.

faq.question: How much does it cost to drive to Orebić from Zagreb?
faq.answer: The motorway toll from Zagreb to the Karamatići exit for Orebić is about €33.70. Because the Pelješac Bridge opened in 2022, no ferry is needed to reach Orebić by road. Fuel is the other main cost on the roughly 600 km route.

faq.question: What is the best time to visit Orebić to save money?
faq.answer: Late May, early June and mid-to-late September give the best mix of lower prices and good weather. The ferry's lower off-season fares apply until 28 May and again from 28 September, and apartment rates are well below the July–August peak.

quickAnswer: Orebić is one of the cheaper Dalmatian coastal bases. Budget travelers can manage on about €60–80 per person per day, mid-range visitors on €100–150, and July–August pushes everything higher. Private rooms start near €30–50 per night, the ferry to Korčula costs €2.50–4.40 one way, and a restaurant main course usually runs €15–28.
